Reasoning: Small-scale clearing doubled with population growth across the basin from 2000 to 2014 [@tyukavina2018congo]. In a national model for 2000 to 2005, population distribution did not predict where forest changed [@kibambelubamba2013modeling].

Pressure: Travel time to Kinshasa and the river landings, by road and river
Reasoning: Across eight Congo Basin countries, from 2000 to 2012, forest clearing fell by 0.63% with each 1% rise in travel time to the nearest market centre [@wheeler2015road].
In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 81.53% of the forest cover changes of 2000 to 2005 lay less than 1 km from existing secondary forest [@kibambelubamba2013modeling].

Each kilometre of first-cut road in the basin was followed by 186 ha of forest loss and degradation [@engert2025explosive]. @engert2025explosive wrote that industrial selective logging there could "degrade forests but lead to little outright deforestation".
About 80% of the deforestation of 2015 to 2020 in the six countries lay within 3 km of the nearest road or settlement [@shapiro2023small].

In Mai Ndombe in 2021, 60% of producers made charcoal from trees felled to open fields [@dubiez2021rapport]. A review found "a mismatch" between wood energy use and forest degradation [@nguba2025assessing].

@ngouhouopoufoun2024cocoa found, among 1,035 households of the Tridom landscape shared by three countries, that "a marginally higher income from cocoa production-based livelihood portfolios is associated with six to seven times higher deforestation". In two pilot sites of Equateur province, @samndong2018institutional found that "shifting cultivation is driven by the poverty conditions of the study area". @behrendt2013deforestation judged that charcoal supply "could represent the single biggest threat to Congo Basin forests in the coming decades".
